content_voiceover: This is the modern, unified view of ITP pathophysiology from Cooper's 2019 New England Journal review, and it's important because it moves past the old teaching that ITP is purely peripheral platelet destruction. There are really two parallel arms happening at once. On the destruction side, cytotoxic T cells directly attack platelets and inhibit megakaryocytes, while B cells, activated through Th cell CD40 to CD154 signaling, differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antiplatelet and antimegakaryocyte autoantibodies. These antibody-coated platelets get recognized by Fc-gamma receptors on splenic and hepatic macrophages, triggering Syk-mediated phagocytosis, that's the classic mechanism everyone learns. But the second arm is production failure, those same autoantibodies bind megakaryocytes and impair their maturation, directly reducing platelet output from the bone marrow, so it isn't just increased peripheral clearance, it's also decreased central production. Layered on top is immune dysregulation, T helper cells are skewed toward Th1 and Th17 inflammatory phenotypes, and regulatory T cell control is impaired, removing the normal brake on this autoimmune process. The board-relevant takeaway is that ITP is a combined disorder of increased destruction and impaired production, which is exactly why TPO receptor agonists, which boost production, work as a distinct treatment mechanism from immunosuppression.
keypoints: ITP = increased platelet destruction PLUS impaired platelet production
Antibody-coated platelets cleared via Fc-gamma receptor phagocytosis (Syk signaling)
Autoantibodies also impair megakaryocyte maturation → reduced production
Th1/Th17 skewing + impaired regulatory T-cell control drive autoimmunity
Dual mechanism explains why TPO-RAs work via a different pathway than steroids
keypoint_voiceover: Remember ITP as a two-hit disease, not just one. Hit one, antibody-coated platelets get phagocytosed by splenic macrophages through Fc-gamma receptors, that's peripheral destruction. Hit two, those same autoantibodies impair megakaryocyte maturation, so the marrow makes fewer platelets to begin with. Add in Th1, Th17 skewing and defective regulatory T cells sustaining the autoimmunity. That's exactly why thrombopoietin receptor agonists, which boost production, are a fundamentally different treatment strategy than steroids, which suppress destruction.
